However, the proposed OVQ-attention algorithm natively operates with a temperature multiplier of exactly $\beta$, exposing an underlying algebraic mismatch between the introductory theory and the desired sequence mixing formula.
* Quote: "= \sum_{n=0}^N c_n e^{-\frac{\beta}{2} ||\mathbf{q}_T - \mu_n^k||^2} \dots"
   * Comment: During the formal proof in Appendix A, the authors silently substitute the previously established $\beta$ coefficient with $\frac{\beta}{2}$ when redefining the exact same conditional expectation for the model. This unexplained mathematical alteration is algebraically mandatory for the final derivation to successfully yield the standard attention equation with the correct temperature scalar. This systemic notational discrepancy is deliberately repeated when comparing the Gaussian Kernel Regression formulations between Equations 11 and 24. By inconsistently manipulating the constants within the Gaussian density functions, the derivations are artificially forced to align with the target attention formula rather than flowing naturally from the stated probabilistic model. Such persistent mathematical inconsistencies substantially undermine the rigor and validity of the formal theoretical foundation proposed for the model.

title: ARGOS: Automated Functional Safety Requirement Synthesis for Embodied AI via Attribute-Guided Combinatorial Reasoning
review:
## Item 1: Contradiction Between "Infinite" Domain Claims and Reliance on a Minimal Curated Rule Base

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The framework claims to solve the scalability issues of traditional safety engineering by handling infinite task possibilities, yet it fundamentally relies on a manually curated, highly constrained rule base of physical attributes.
* Evaluation criteria: Conclusions

#### Evidence
* Quote: "To tackle the challenge of infinite task possibilities, ARGOS moves beyond the traditional reliance on pre-defined function lists."
   * Comment: The authors criticize traditional HARA for relying on finite function lists, yet their own framework relies on a similarly finite and manually curated rule base of physical attributes. Appendix B lists only about 21 rules spanning users, environments, and tasks. It is highly unlikely that this small set of predefined rules can cover the infinite task possibilities or the open-ended nature of general embodied AI instructions. The reliance on this static rule base simply shifts the enumeration bottleneck from hazard scenarios to physical attributes, fundamentally limiting the framework's scalability and contradicting its core motivation. To truly support an open-world setting, the system would need a dynamic mechanism to acquire or infer attributes for entirely novel entities, which is absent here.
* Quote: "The target Rule Base R is initialized through expert curation to ensure strict adherence to physical laws; representative examples of these rules are provided in Appendix B. While this represents a one-time engineering cost, it decouples atomic physical constraints from specific scenarios, allowing the pipeline to automatically synthesize an unbounded number of complex interaction risks without further human intervention."
   * Comment: Claiming that the pipeline can synthesize an unbounded number of complex interaction risks from this finite rule base is mathematically and practically overstated. While combinatorial combinations of 21 rules yield a larger space, it is strictly bounded and fails to generalize to novel entities or attributes not present in the curated base. When evaluating against open-world scenarios, an LLM acting strictly upon these few injected attributes will inevitably miss out-of-distribution physical constraints. A more realistic assessment of the rule base's coverage limitations is necessary to substantiate the system's deployment viability. Without evaluating on scenarios that require rules outside the curated subset, the generalizability of the combinatorial reasoning module remains unproven.



## Item 2: Absence of External Knowledge Retrieval Baselines for Fair Comparison

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The experimental evaluation fails to compare the proposed method against existing LLM-based hazard analysis frameworks, only benchmarking against prompting variations of the same model.
* Evaluation criteria: Originality and significance

#### Evidence
* Quote: "Recent research has begun to integrate LLMs into the hazard analysis pipeline. Frameworks like Aegis (Shi et al., 2024), Co-Hazard Analysis (Diemert & Weber, 2023), and prompt-layered approaches (Iyenghar et al., 2025) utilize LLMs as “expert surrogates” to streamline the generation of safety documentation or map identified hazards to regulations (Nouri et al., 2024)."
   * Comment: The experimental setup completely omits empirical comparisons against other contemporary LLM-based safety analysis frameworks mentioned in the related work. By only comparing the proposed method against basic zero-shot and chain-of-thought prompting variants of the same LLM, the evaluation is heavily skewed. This effectively only proves that retrieval-augmented generation using physical rules is better than no retrieval at all. Such an outcome is a well-known phenomenon in NLP and does not adequately establish the superiority of the ARGOS architecture itself. To claim state-of-the-art performance in automated hazard analysis, the authors must benchmark against existing frameworks designed for similar tasks.
* Quote: "Vanilla LLM: This baseline represents the model’s intrinsic safety knowledge. It is prompted to generate hazard scenarios based solely on the seed description and the robot’s capability profile, without any intermediate reasoning steps or external attribute grounding."
   * Comment: While the authors argue that prior methods operate on finite functional scopes, they could have adapted these methods' retrieval modules for a fair comparison. Alternatively, they could have compared against a standard semantic retrieval-augmented generation baseline that queries generic safety guidelines rather than their curated attribute rule base. Without a baseline that also uses external knowledge retrieval, it is impossible to determine the true source of the performance gains. Readers cannot know whether the improvements stem from the novel combinatorial reasoning or merely from the injection of external context. Introducing a standard retrieval baseline would significantly strengthen the empirical claims regarding the necessity of explicit attribute-based deduction.



## Item 3: Lack of Formal Mathematical Definitions for Custom Topological Evaluation Metrics

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The paper introduces custom geometric and statistical metrics for evaluating semantic topology without providing the formal mathematical equations required to compute them.
* Evaluation criteria: Data and methodology

#### Evidence
* Quote: "We report the Effective Rank (Eff. Rank) to estimate the intrinsic dimensionality of the scenario manifold, and Centroid Shift (Shift) to quantify the Euclidean deviation from the seed’s Operational Design Domain (ODD)."
   * Comment: The authors introduce complex-sounding geometric metrics such as Effective Rank and Centroid Shift without specifying how they are mathematically computed from the embeddings. For instance, computing an effective rank can be done via singular value decomposition entropy or thresholding, but the exact formulation is absent. Without a precise formula, it is impossible for independent researchers to replicate the dimensionality estimation. Furthermore, researchers cannot verify if the chosen metric is appropriate for the specific properties of the high-dimensional embeddings used in the study. Relying purely on textual descriptions for advanced statistical measures introduces unacceptable ambiguity into the evaluation.
* Quote: "Constrained Semantic Expansion (CSE), defined as the ratio of internal diversity to centroid shift (Diversity/Drift), which evaluates exploration efficiency; and Directional Similarity, calculated as the average cosine similarity of difference vectors relative to the seed"
   * Comment: Similarly, Constrained Semantic Expansion relies on internal diversity, a term that is never mathematically defined in the text. It is unclear if this diversity refers to the average pairwise Euclidean distance, the trace of the covariance matrix, or an entirely different geometric property. The description for Directional Similarity references difference vectors relative to the seed, but does not clarify whether these are calculated per generated scenario or globally. Additionally, the aggregation method for these difference vectors remains completely unspecified. The lack of rigorous equations for custom evaluation metrics severely compromises the reproducibility of the quantitative claims made in Table 3.



## Item 4: Missing Inter-Rater Reliability Metrics for Subjective Human Evaluations

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The human evaluation lacks reporting on inter-rater reliability metrics, and the demographics or expertise of the human evaluators are entirely omitted.
* Evaluation criteria: Appropriate use of statistics and treatment of uncertainties

#### Evidence
* Quote: "We randomly sampled N = 108 derived scenarios across three methods (Ours, CoT, Vanilla)."
   * Comment: While the paper mentions sampling 108 derived scenarios, it fails to specify how these samples are distributed across the three evaluated methods. It is standard practice to state whether this was a stratified sample ensuring exactly 36 scenarios per method, or a purely random draw that could skew the aggregated metrics. Furthermore, there is no mention of the specific qualifications, affiliations, or potential conflicts of interest of the three human reviewers. This information is critical when evaluating a highly specialized and subjective domain like functional safety engineering. Without these demographics, it is impossible to gauge the expertise level driving the human baseline scores.
* Quote: "To mitigate subjective bias, the final human score is reported as the average of the three human reviewers, and we analyze the inter-rater agreement and human-AI alignment in Section 4.2."
   * Comment: The authors claim they analyze the inter-rater agreement, but no standard inter-rater reliability metrics are reported anywhere in the paper. Established metrics such as Fleiss' Kappa or Krippendorff's Alpha are essential to prove that human judges agreed on the subjective safety assessments. Stating that an analysis was performed without providing the statistical results leaves readers unable to judge the consistency of the annotations. In subjective evaluations on a 1-to-10 scale, human variance can be quite high, which heavily influences the reported averages. Without a formal measure of agreement, the validity of the human benchmark, and the subsequent claims of LLM-to-human alignment, remains highly questionable.



## Item 5: Inappropriate Use of Algebraic Notation to Describe Heuristic Prompt Templates

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The methodology misleadingly employs formal mathematical operators to describe what is essentially simple string formatting within a prompt template.
* Evaluation criteria: Clarity and context

#### Evidence
* Quote: "Formally, for a set of k risk factors {u1, . . . , uk}, the hazard mechanism Hdesc is derived as:"
   * Comment: The authors attempt to formalize their prompt construction by presenting an equation that uses a mathematical operator to define the hazard mechanism generation. In mathematics and machine learning, such symbols typically denote specific algebraic operations like Kronecker products on vectors or matrices. Here, the notation is used merely to represent the concatenation or co-occurrence of textual attributes within a language model prompt. This kind of pseudo-mathematics degrades the clarity of the paper and can confuse readers attempting to implement the system mathematically rather than textually. Using rigorous mathematical framing for non-mathematical string manipulation practices reduces the manuscript's overall scientific rigor.
* Quote: "The core novelty of our method lies in the Risk Injection Block. We retrieve two complementary risk factors (RA, RB) and inject them into the following template."
   * Comment: When referencing the actual implementation in Appendix A.1, the operator is revealed to be a simple text template explicitly listing "Risk Factor A:" and "Risk Factor B:". Portraying string interpolation as a formal mathematical operator overcomplicates a standard prompt engineering technique. Papers in the field of LLM applications should strive for transparency by directly describing their prompt construction rather than dressing up heuristics in algebraic notation. The authors should replace the pseudo-mathematical equation with a clear text-based description of how the attributes are formulated in the context window. Such an adjustment would make the framework much easier for practitioners to understand and replicate without deciphering overloaded mathematical symbols.

title: Private PoEtry: Private In-Context Learning via Product of Experts
review:
## Item 1: Invalid convergence proof due to mathematical error in Theorem 3.4

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The proof of Theorem 3.4 contains a fundamental algebraic error where the scalar factor $J$ (the number of in-context examples) is incorrectly dropped from the softmax exponent. This invalidates the claim that the Product-of-Experts approximation converges to a smooth full-context distribution, as the distribution actually collapses to a degenerate one-hot point mass as $J \to \infty$.
* Evaluation criteria: Conclusions
* Component of the paper: Section 3.2, Theorem 3.4 and its proof

#### Evidence
* Quote: `pJ (y | x, C1:J ) = exp(J · uJ (y)) / \sum_{y'} exp(J · uJ (y')) = exp(uJ (y) − uJ (ymax)) / \sum_{y'} exp(uJ (y') − uJ (ymax)). (8)`
   * Comment: The second equality in this equation is algebraically incorrect because the scalar $J$ inside the exponential cannot be eliminated. Factoring out $\exp(J \cdot u_J(y_{max}))$ from both the numerator and the denominator yields $\exp(J(u_J(y) - u_J(y_{max})))$, which strictly retains the $J$ multiplier in the exponent. 
* Quote: `pJ (y) = softmax(vJ )y \xrightarrow{a.s.} softmax(v\star)y = p\star(y | x,S).`
   * Comment: Because the $J$ factor was erroneously omitted in Equation 8, this final step of the proof is invalid. The actual normalized probability $p_J$ is the softmax of $J \cdot v_J$, not $v_J$. Since $v^*(y) < 0$ for any non-argmax $y$, the term $J \cdot v_J(y)$ diverges to $-\infty$ as $J \to \infty$. Consequently, the true limiting distribution collapses to a one-hot point mass centered on the most likely token, contradicting the claim that it converges to the smooth limiting distribution $p^\star$.



## Item 2: Flawed formal definition of the clipping function

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The formal definitions of the clipping operation for log-probabilities are fundamentally incorrect. As written, the function artificially maximizes the likelihood of highly improbable tokens, which would invert and destroy the model's predictive utility.
* Evaluation criteria: Data and methodology
* Component of the paper: Section 3.1 and Appendix B.1

#### Evidence
* Quote: `The clipping-operator clipγ (l) passes values li ∈ [−γ, 0] unchanged and sets all other values to zero.`
   * Comment: Log-probabilities from a language model are strictly negative or zero. This text explicitly states that if a log-probability $l_i$ is less than $-\gamma$, it is set to $0$. However, a log-probability of $0$ corresponds to a probability of $1$, which is the maximum possible value. Consequently, this operation would incorrectly map the most unlikely tokens to the highest possible probability.
* Quote: `For scalar l: clipγ (l) = l if − γ ≤ l ≤ 0 , 0 otherwise`
   * Comment: This mathematical formalization in Appendix B.1 repeats the same error. To properly bound the sensitivity without inverting the utility, the clipping function should floor small log-probabilities at $-\gamma$ (e.g., return $-\gamma$ when $l < -\gamma$), maintaining their status as low-probability events. While Appendix C implies a lower bound of $e^{-\gamma}$ on probabilities, the explicit mathematical definition provided here is critically flawed.



## Item 3: Contradictory and invalid Membership Inference Attack evaluation

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The methodology for the Membership Inference Attack (MIA) is flawed because it evaluates an internal, un-noised variable (the aggregated logits) rather than the final differentially private output, violating the defined threat model and undermining the empirical privacy claims.
* Evaluation criteria: Conclusions
* Component of the paper: Section 4.4 and Appendix E.2

#### Evidence
* Quote: `that this is a simulated version of in-context learning, where only the class prediction is output, not its logits.`
   * Comment: This sentence correctly acknowledges that in the proposed differentially private setup (and per Algorithm 1), the system only exposes the final sampled token (the hard label) to the user. A valid empirical privacy evaluation of the DP mechanism must therefore operate strictly on these exposed class predictions, typically via a label-only MIA.
* Quote: `The attack scenario is as follows: the context is loaded with data from N private data sources; the attacker can input any query and will receive a predicted class and its logits.`
   * Comment: This directly contradicts the preceding statement by granting the attacker access to the internal logits (the aggregated utility scores before the exponential mechanism sampling). The DP guarantee provided by the algorithm applies exclusively to the final sampled token, not to these intermediate utility scores. By performing a likelihood-ratio attack on these internal scores, the evaluation bypasses the DP boundary entirely, making the resulting AUROC values invalid for assessing the true empirical privacy of the deployed mechanism.

title: Instance-Free Domain Adaptive Object Detection
review:
## Item 1: Unfair evaluation against self-training baselines

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: I am criticizing the paper for conducting an unfair and misleading baseline evaluation by applying self-training methods to target data known to contain no foreground instances. This criticism refers to the "Performance Comparison" component of the paper, specifically the evaluation of the AT and CAT baselines.
* Evaluation criteria: Validity and Conclusions.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "The teacher-student frameworks suffer from a performance collapse, as erroneous pseudo-labels on background-only target images cause the student to learn incorrect foreground representations."
   * Comment: The authors explicitly acknowledge that teacher-student frameworks collapse because they generate false pseudo-labels on background-only images. However, applying these methods out-of-the-box to a dataset explicitly defined as containing zero foreground instances guarantees this exact failure mode. Self-training methods like AT and CAT are fundamentally designed to discover and align foreground objects in the target domain, assuming their presence. Demonstrating that these methods fail when applied to purely background images is a trivial, engineered, and predictable outcome. A scientifically valid baseline comparison would not penalize existing methods for failing in a scenario they were never configured to handle without appropriate modifications.
* Quote: "Instance-Free DAOD operates under a stricter information constraint on the target domain: during training, the available target data are instance-free images that contain only background."
   * Comment: Because the proposed "Instance-Free DAOD" setting assumes the practitioner knows the target data is exclusively background, any deployed baseline should be adapted to respect this constraint. A fair evaluation would modify the self-training baselines by disabling pseudo-label generation on the target set and using the target images strictly for adversarial background alignment. By failing to adapt these baselines to the known absence of target instances, the paper evaluates them unfairly against the proposed RSCN. This oversight severely undermines the validity of the reported empirical gains. Consequently, the performance degradation of the self-training baselines is a methodological artifact rather than a genuine reflection of their adaptability.


## Item 2: Geometric redundancy of the Relative Space Harmonization (RSH) loss

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: I am criticizing the paper for introducing a mathematically redundant loss function that does not harmonize cross-domain relative geometry, but instead merely forces target background prototypes to equal source background prototypes. This criticism refers to the "Relative Space Harmonization (RSH)" component of the proposed RSCN method.
* Evaluation criteria: Validity and Conclusions.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "The source-domain relative vector is computed as $d_c^s = N(p_c^s - p_{bg}^s)$ and the cross-domain relative vector is computed as $d_c^t = N(p_c^s - p_{bg}^t)$."
   * Comment: This formulation defines the relative vectors by anchoring both the source and target background prototypes to the exact same source foreground prototype, $p_c^s$. The function $N(\cdot)$ applies an L2 normalization, meaning that these relative vectors represent only the multi-dimensional direction from the background prototype to the foreground prototype. By sharing $p_c^s$, the vectors $d_c^s$ and $d_c^t$ are intrinsically tied to the source domain's spatial structure. Consequently, any optimization applied to the difference between these vectors will primarily constrain the position of the target background prototype relative to the source background. This mathematical setup fails to introduce any independent target foreground information into the relative geometry.
* Quote: "Then we propose the RSH loss, encouraging the geometric consistency by minimizing the distance between these two relative vectors:"
   * Comment: The RSH loss minimizes the absolute distance between the directional vectors computed in the previous step. Geometrically, for a single class $c$, forcing $d_c^s = d_c^t$ implies that $p_{bg}^t$ must lie on the precise ray originating from $p_c^s$ and passing through $p_{bg}^s$. Because this constraint is summed over multiple non-collinear foreground class prototypes in $C(x^s)$, the only point $p_{bg}^t$ that can simultaneously satisfy all these distinct ray equations is their exact intersection point, $p_{bg}^s$. Therefore, the RSH constraint does not learn novel cross-domain relationships but merely provides an indirect, mathematically redundant penalty forcing $p_{bg}^t = p_{bg}^s$. This renders the module practically identical in objective to the primary Background Prototype Alignment (BPA) loss.


## Item 3: Methodological flaw in extracting target background prototypes via RPN

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: I am criticizing the paper for a flawed methodological design choice in constructing the target background prototype using RPN proposals, which inherently biases the representation towards hard negatives rather than a representative global background. This criticism refers to the "Background Prototype Alignment (BPA)" component of the methodology.
* Evaluation criteria: Data and methodology, and Validity.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "Concretely, we extract average-pooled instance-level proposal features from the RPN of the Faster R-CNN detector G."
   * Comment: The Region Proposal Network (RPN) in the Faster R-CNN architecture is explicitly optimized to propose bounding boxes that have a high probability of containing foreground objects. It achieves this by identifying regions with high "objectness" scores, effectively filtering out obvious background areas. When applied to any image, the RPN prioritizes distinct textures, sharp edges, or structures that resemble the objects it was trained to detect. Consequently, the proposals extracted by the RPN do not represent a random or uniform sampling of the image content. Relying on these proposals means the feature extraction process is heavily biased towards object-like characteristics rather than general environmental context.
* Quote: "For target-domain images, which contain no foreground instances, we simply average all proposals to obtain a background prototype $p_{bg}^t$."
   * Comment: Because the target-domain images consist entirely of background, the RPN will naturally output proposals centered on hard negatives or deceptive clutter that most resemble foreground objects. By averaging all of these specific, false-positive-leaning proposals, the resulting target prototype $p_{bg}^t$ fails to capture the true marginal background distribution of the target domain. Instead, it aggregates an adversarial subset of edge cases that the detector already struggles with. Aligning this highly biased representation with the source domain introduces a severe inductive bias that misrepresents the true target domain statistics. This flawed methodological choice fundamentally challenges the validity of the resulting cross-domain adaptation strategy.


## Item 4: Missing implementation details for source background prototype extraction

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: I am criticizing the paper for omitting critical implementation details regarding the extraction and filtering of the source background prototype, severely hindering reproducibility. This criticism refers to the "Relational and Structural Consistency Network" component, specifically the formulation of the source background prototype $p_{bg}^s$.
* Evaluation criteria: Data and methodology.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "For source-domain images in a batch, we average proposals according to their ground-truth categories to form foreground prototypes $\{p_c^s\}_{c \in C(x^s)}, p_c^s \in \mathbb{R}^d$, together with a source background prototype $p_{bg}^s \in \mathbb{R}^d$."
   * Comment: The paper describes the formation of foreground prototypes by grouping RPN proposals according to their ground-truth categories, which provides a clear and reproducible strategy for object classes. However, the text completely fails to explain the parallel process used to compute the source background prototype, $p_{bg}^s$. Standard object detection pipelines define background proposals based on an Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold with ground-truth objects, typically classifying regions with an IoU below 0.3 as negative. The authors do not state whether $p_{bg}^s$ is formed by averaging all such negative proposals, randomly sampling a subset of them, or employing a completely different extraction strategy. This critical omission leaves the exact nature of the source background representation entirely undefined.
* Quote: "Here $C(x^s)$ denotes the set of foreground class indices present in $x^s$, bg is the index of the background class, and d is the feature dimension."
   * Comment: The entire foundation of the Background Prototype Alignment (BPA) and Relative Space Harmonization (RSH) relies on computing distances involving this undefined source background prototype, $p_{bg}^s$. Because the cross-domain alignment depends entirely on the spatial characteristics of this feature vector, any ambiguity in its construction is highly problematic for the paper's scientific rigor. If different researchers make different assumptions about how the background proposals are filtered and pooled, they will obtain drastically different prototype vectors, leading to divergent alignment behaviors. Without explicitly defining the criteria for filtering and selecting these source background features, the methodology is critically incomplete. Consequently, the reported experiments and adaptation mechanisms cannot be accurately reproduced by independent researchers.


## Item 5: Unjustified SSP constraint compared to standard feature distillation

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: I am criticizing the paper for failing to justify the proposed SSP constraint against standard, widely adopted knowledge distillation baselines used for preventing feature collapse. This criticism refers to the "Source Structure Preservation (SSP)" component of the methodology and the corresponding ablation studies.
* Evaluation criteria: Originality and significance, and Validity.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "Without such regularization, the feature space remains vulnerable to structural degradation during adaptation (Su et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2021), potentially leading to feature collapse where categories become indistinguishable."
   * Comment: The problem of preventing feature collapse and maintaining discriminability on the source domain during adaptation is heavily studied in domain adaptation and continual learning. This degradation is typically mitigated using well-established knowledge distillation approaches, which enforce consistency between the adapting model and a pre-trained model. These standard approaches include minimizing the L2 distance between intermediate feature maps or the KL divergence between output logits of the adapting model and a frozen source model. Because these techniques are computationally efficient and widely adopted as industry standards, they serve as the natural baselines for any new method claiming to prevent structural degradation. Proposing a novel regularization technique requires demonstrating its superiority over these existing, foundational methods.
* Quote: "To address this, we introduce Source Structure Preservation (SSP) to regularize the intrinsic discriminative structure of the source features."
   * Comment: The proposed SSP method introduces a more complex regularization involving the computation of inter-class cosine similarity matrices from a frozen reference detector. However, the authors completely omit comparisons to the aforementioned standard knowledge distillation baselines in their ablation studies or main results. Without demonstrating that SSP outperforms or provides unique empirical benefits over conventional feature distillation, the necessity of this specific constraint remains entirely unsupported. The added computational overhead of computing prototype similarity matrices per batch is not justified if a simple L2 feature penalty achieves identical structural preservation. Therefore, the originality and significance of the SSP module are highly questionable given the lack of rigorous baseline benchmarking.

title: Bird-SR: Bidirectional Reward-Guided Diffusion for Real-World Image Super-Resolution
review:
## Item 1: Flawed Formulation of the Unpaired Preference Loss

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The preference loss function defined for the unpaired objective incorrectly minimizes the absolute reward score rather than maximizing it, reversing the intended optimization goal.
* Evaluation criteria: Validity

#### Evidence
* Quote: "We define the image at timestep $t = 0$ and the loss form is written as: $\mathcal{L}_{\text{unpair}} = \mathbb{E}_{t}\big [\phi(r(\hat{x}_0)) \big ]$"
   * Comment: The explicit goal of this unpaired preference loss is to maximize the reward function $r(\hat{x}_0)$, which serves as a proxy for perceptual quality. In standard optimization, an objective function meant to be maximized must either be negated or appropriately transformed before applying gradient descent. However, the authors define this loss by applying the preference function directly to the raw reward score without any inversion. Consequently, the optimization process is mathematically instructed to minimize the absolute reward score. This fundamental error completely reverses the intended optimization direction, effectively penalizing the model for generating high-quality images.
* Quote: "For the reward function r, we employ ClipiQA; for the distortion metric D, we adopt LPIPS; and for the preference loss function $\phi$, we use ReLU."
   * Comment: The paper states that the ClipIQA metric is used as the reward signal, which inherently outputs positive scores bounded between zero and one. Because the preference loss function $\phi$ is specified as a standard ReLU operation, any positive ClipIQA score will pass through unchanged, resulting in $\max(0, \text{ClipIQA}) = \text{ClipIQA}$. When the gradient descent optimizer attempts to minimize this $\mathcal{L}_{\text{unpair}}$ objective, it will directly push the ClipIQA score toward zero. This means the model is actively trained to degrade the perceptual quality of the generated images, completely undermining the core motivation of reward feedback learning. Such a flawed formulation renders the unpaired optimization strategy conceptually invalid.



## Item 2: Contradiction in Dynamic Distortion-Perception Weighting

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The mathematical definition and visualization of the dynamic weighting schedule completely contradict the paper's stated logic of assigning higher emphasis to distortion at early timesteps.
* Evaluation criteria: Conclusions

#### Evidence
* Quote: "The weight $\lambda(t) \in [0, 1]$ is a monotonically decreasing function of timestep $t$, assigning higher emphasis to distortion at early timesteps and gradually shifting focus toward perceptual rewards at later stages."
   * Comment: In the context of the reverse diffusion process, early generation stages correspond to large $t$ values, where high noise levels preserve only global structures. The text explicitly claims that $\lambda(t)$ should decrease as the timestep $t$ increases. This theoretical design would correctly assign a low weight to the perceptual loss at these early stages. Consequently, the distortion loss, weighted by $1-\lambda(t)$, would receive a high emphasis when reconstructing global structures. This logical progression aligns perfectly with the stated goal of stabilizing structural fidelity before injecting fine-grained perceptual details.
* Quote: "$\lambda(t) = (t/T)^\gamma$, which gradually shifts from distortion to perceptual reward"
   * Comment: Despite the logical reasoning provided in the text, the mathematical formulation defines the weighting schedule as an exponentially growing function. Because $t$ ranges from $0$ to $T$ and $\gamma$ is positive, the term $(t/T)^\gamma$ is strictly monotonically increasing with respect to $t$. As visually confirmed by the plotted curves in Figure 6, at the earliest generative stages ($t=T=40$), $\lambda(t)$ evaluates to $1.0$. This completely removes the distortion penalty since $1-1=0$, and instead applies maximum weight to the perceptual reward. This implementation acts in direct opposition to the paper's stated methodological goal, exposing a severe contradiction in the framework's core design.



## Item 3: Contradictory Ablation Claims for the ResShift Model

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The textual claims regarding the ablation study for the ResShift model falsely report an improvement in perceptual quality that is directly contradicted by the table's empirical data.
* Evaluation criteria: Conclusions

#### Evidence
* Quote: "As presented in Table 6, utilizing solely the reward signal without additional constraints leads to a significant improvement in perceptual metrics... Ultimately, by integrating both constraints, our model achieves a stable and synergistic improvement across both perceptual quality and distortion metrics."
   * Comment: In Section 10.1, the authors discuss the ablation results on loss components for the ResShift model, which are detailed in Table 6. The text confidently claims that integrating both structural and semantic constraints alongside the reward signal yields a synergistic improvement across metrics. This statement suggests that the FULL model variant optimally balances structural fidelity with superior perceptual realism. The narrative implies that adding the reward signal is strictly beneficial when properly regularized. However, a close inspection of the empirical data directly invalidates this descriptive narrative.
* Quote: "FULL | $\checkmark$ | $\checkmark$ | $\checkmark$ | 0.465 | 0.314"
   * Comment: According to the data in Table 6, the FULL model achieves a ClipIQA score of $0.465$, which is intended to measure perceptual quality. In stark contrast, Model C, which entirely omits the reward loss, achieves a higher ClipIQA score of $0.472$. Thus, adding the reward signal actually degrades the perceptual quality of the generated output for the ResShift model. The authors appear to have erroneously duplicated the text from the DiT4SR analysis in Section 5.3.3 without adjusting for the different outcomes. This misrepresentation creates a misleading conclusion regarding the universal effectiveness of the proposed loss combination.



## Item 4: Undefined Variable and Ambiguous Reverse Trajectory in Algorithm 1

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: Algorithm 1 relies on an undefined variable to dictate the span of the reverse optimization trajectory, making the core real-world training loop ambiguous and irreproducible.
* Evaluation criteria: Data and methodology

#### Evidence
* Quote: "for $t = T$ to $t = j + 2$ do"
   * Comment: Algorithm 1 provides the foundational pseudo-code for the proposed bidirectional reward-guided diffusion framework. Lines 11 through 13 define a loop that executes the reverse diffusion process without computing gradients. The bounds of this iterative loop are determined by the maximum timestep $T$ and a target threshold defined as $j + 2$. This mechanism is critical for establishing the starting point of the single-step optimization phase. However, the variable $j$ is never initialized, sampled, or explicitly defined anywhere within the algorithm or the surrounding textual description.
* Quote: "with grad: $x_j \leftarrow x_{j+1}$"
   * Comment: Following the gradient-free loop, the algorithm performs a single gradient update using the state variables corresponding to index $j$. Because the value or distribution of $j$ is completely undefined, it is impossible to determine which specific timestep along the reverse trajectory is actually being optimized. While Section 4.2 briefly mentions focusing on the 'last timestep', this qualitative remark does not resolve the mathematical ambiguity of the pseudo-code. Without explicitly knowing how $j$ is selected or derived, an independent researcher cannot reliably reconstruct the proposed training pipeline. This critical omission severely hinders the methodological transparency and reproducibility of the paper.



## Item 5: Inconsistent Reporting of Improvements in the Results Table

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The quantitative reporting in Table 1 contains systematic arithmetic and formatting errors that misleadingly portray performance deteriorations as improvements for the LPIPS metric.
* Evaluation criteria: Appropriate use of statistics and treatment of uncertainties

#### Evidence
* Quote: "Orange subscripts indicate improvement ($\uparrow \Delta$) over baselines (2 d.p.)."
   * Comment: Table 1 summarizes the quantitative results across multiple benchmarks, utilizing color-coded subscripts to highlight performance deltas. The caption explicitly defines the orange subscript and the accompanying up-arrow symbol as indicators of a positive performance improvement over the baseline models. This formatting choice is designed to allow readers to quickly identify where the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results. Such visual cues must be rigorously verified to ensure they accurately reflect the underlying mathematical differences. Unfortunately, this convention is incorrectly applied to metrics where lower values correspond to better performance.
* Quote: "0.353 [Baseline LPIPS] ... 0.362($\uparrow$ 0.00) [w/ Ours LPIPS]"
   * Comment: For the LPIPS metric, where a lower score indicates superior perceptual quality, an increase in value represents a deterioration in model performance. In Table 1, the LPIPS score for the ResShift model on the DrealSR dataset increases from a baseline of $0.353$ to $0.362$ with the proposed method. This shift reflects a clear performance degradation of $0.009$, yet the table falsely labels it with an orange '$\uparrow 0.00$' subscript. A similar arithmetic and formatting error occurs for the DiT4SR model on the RealSR dataset, where a $0.009$ improvement is bizarrely reported as '$\uparrow 0.02$'. These inconsistent calculations and misleading visual indicators severely compromise the statistical reliability of the reported results.

title: When Shared Knowledge Hurts: Spectral Over-Accumulation in Model Merging
review:
## Item 1: Unfair baseline comparison due to disabling global scaling

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The experimental methodology artificially handicaps the baseline merging methods by forcing a fixed global scaling factor ($\lambda=1$), which contradicts standard practices and artificially inflates the relative improvements achieved by the proposed method.
* Evaluation criteria: Data and methodology.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "Although prior work (Ilharco et al., 2022; Yadav et al., 2023) relies on an additional hyperparameter $\lambda$ to integrate the task update and pre-trained weight, we keep $\lambda = 1$ throughout our experiments."
   * Comment: Standard practice for Task Arithmetic, TIES, and DARE requires tuning the global scaling factor $\lambda$ (typically setting $\lambda < 1$) to prevent the combined task updates from exploding in magnitude, which inherently causes severe performance degradation. By forcing $\lambda = 1$, the authors evaluate artificially crippled baselines that suffer from extreme weight over-accumulation. Since Singular Value Calibration (SVC) implicitly shrinks singular values (acting as an adaptive scaling factor), its large reported improvements (e.g., +13.0% over Task Arithmetic) largely just recover the performance loss caused by disabling the baseline's necessary $\lambda$ tuning. This makes the empirical comparison unfair and heavily overstates the true relative benefit of SVC compared to properly scaled baselines.
* Quote: "The hyperparameters used in previous methods remain identical to those specified in their original papers."
   * Comment: This statement directly contradicts the decision to fix $\lambda = 1$ outlined in the Appendix. The original papers for Task Arithmetic and TIES explicitly define $\lambda$ as a tunable hyperparameter essential for multi-task merging, and their reported results rely heavily on sweeping it. Claiming to use the identical hyperparameters as the original papers while quietly overriding the most critical scaling parameter in the Appendix constitutes a severe methodological inconsistency. As a result, the baseline accuracies presented (e.g., 68.9% for Task Arithmetic on ViT-B/32) are significantly lower than those achieved by the properly tuned methods in the literature.


## Item 2: Severe numerical instability in the projection coefficient formulation

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The unweighted mathematical formulation for the subspace calibration factor is highly susceptible to numerical instability, where a task with near-zero capability in a subspace can erroneously drive the calibration factor to zero and suppress valid spectral components.
* Evaluation criteria: Validity.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "s_i^r = \frac{\langle a_{\text{merge}}^r, a_i^r \rangle}{\|a_i^r\|_2^2}"
   * Comment: In practical model merging scenarios, such as when combining sparse task updates (e.g., DARE) or entirely disjoint tasks, a given task $i$ may have virtually zero projection along a subspace $r$, meaning $\|a_i^r\|_2 \to 0$. In this scenario, the denominator of the projection coefficient approaches zero, while random alignments in high-dimensional spaces cause the numerator to shrink at a slower linear rate. Consequently, floating-point division will cause the computed coefficient $s_i^r$ to erroneously explode to an arbitrarily large value. The paper provides no mathematical or algorithmic safeguard—such as additive smoothing or magnitude-based weighting—to handle tasks that are inactive in a specific spectral subspace.
* Quote: "\gamma^r = K / \sum_{i=1}^K \max(\alpha, s_i^r)."
   * Comment: Because the final subspace calibration factor $\gamma^r$ is computed using an unweighted harmonic mean of the individual task coefficients, a single spuriously large $s_i^r$ from an inactive task will dominate the entire sum. This numerical instability causes the denominator to explode, driving $\gamma^r$ to near zero and completely suppressing the singular value $\tilde{\sigma}^r$ for all tasks. This implies that the proposed unweighted aggregation is highly fragile and will destructively zero out valid spectral subspaces whenever at least one merged task lacks capability in that specific direction.


## Item 3: Test-set overfitting of the calibration hyperparameter

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The selection of the critical hyperparameter $\alpha$ constitutes test-set overfitting, which violates the claim of a completely "data-free" method and undermines the reliability of the empirical results.
* Evaluation criteria: Data and methodology.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "The hyperparameters introduced in this paper are set to $\alpha = 1/K$ by default... However, for TSV-M w/ SVC, we set $\alpha = 1$ by default (the most stable, suppression-only setting)..."
   * Comment: The authors promote Singular Value Calibration as a "training-free and data-free post-processing method," which implies it can be applied universally without relying on validation data. However, they manually alter the critical hyperparameter $\alpha$ depending on the base merging method, reverting to $\alpha = 1$ specifically for TSV-M to avoid overestimating correction coefficients. Selecting hyperparameters based on which configuration yields the highest test-set accuracy for a specific baseline constitutes data leakage and test-set overfitting. This undermines the claim that the method requires no data, as the default parameters were implicitly tuned against the evaluation benchmarks.
* Quote: "Fig. 5 shows that $\alpha = 1$ yields consistent gains... In contrast, additionally boosting singular values ($\alpha \in (0, 1)$) requires caution and can degrade performance as $\alpha$ decreases."
   * Comment: This observation explicitly acknowledges that smaller values of $\alpha$ (such as their default $1/K$) can destabilize the spectral balance and degrade performance, making the choice of $\alpha$ highly sensitive. Without a principled, data-free heuristic or a separate validation set to tune this parameter, deploying $\alpha = 1/K$ across all other baselines simply because it empirically maximized their final benchmark scores is methodologically flawed. A truly data-free method must apply a uniform, un-tuned rule, whereas this approach masks the inherent instability of the proposed amplification mechanism by selectively toggling it off when it fails.

title: Rethinking Weight Tying: Pseudo-Inverse Tying for Stable LM Training and Updates
review:
## Item 1: Conclusion contradicts empirical results

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: I am criticizing the paper for incorrectly concluding that PIT provides consistent performance improvements, blatantly contradicting its own experimental data which shows severe degradation in most cases. This criticism refers to Section 5.3 (Results on LM Pre-Training) and Table 1.
* Evaluation criteria: Conclusions

#### Evidence
* Quote: "Analysis. The improvements are modest but consistent across scales, supporting the view that PIT acts primarily as a stabilizing inductive bias."
   * Comment: Table 1 clearly contradicts these claims. For four out of the six evaluated models, PIT results in substantially higher training loss and perplexity (PPI) compared to the standard weight tying (TT) baseline. Most notably, in all three scratch-mode models, PIT's perplexity is nearly three times higher than that of TT (e.g., Llama-1.17B perplexity increases from 18.303 to 64.984). Furthermore, in teacher-mode, the GPT-590M model also experiences a noticeable performance drop, with PPI increasing from 33.892 to 41.027. Describing these severe regressions as "modest but consistent" improvements is a significant misinterpretation of the empirical data.
* Quote: "We evaluate PIT on compact LMs spanning 256M-1.3B parameters across pretraining and adaptation, and consistently observe improved training stability, stronger layerwise semantic consistency, and substantially reduced side effects."
   * Comment: The abstract explicitly asserts that PIT consistently improves training stability and reduces side effects across all evaluated models. However, this generalized claim is entirely unsupported by the primary pretraining results presented in Table 1. Achieving a stable but vastly inferior loss plateau—as seen with the scratch models—cannot be reasonably characterized as an improvement in training stability. By completely omitting the negative results from their high-level summaries, the authors present a skewed and unreliable conclusion. A scientifically rigorous abstract must accurately reflect both the successes and the prominent failures of the proposed method.



## Item 2: Flawed methodology for scratch-mode training

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: I am criticizing the paper for a flawed experimental design where the shared token memory is frozen to a random matrix, unfairly crippling the model's capacity to learn token semantics. This criticism refers to Section 5.2 (Implementation Details) and the scratch-mode experiments.
* Evaluation criteria: Data and methodology

#### Evidence
* Quote: "In scratch-mode, we initialize $Z$ as a random Stiefel matrix. Unless otherwise noted, we freeze $Z$ after initialization, so all interface adaptation happens through the learned SPD transform."
   * Comment: Standard language models train the full vocabulary embedding matrix to capture the rich semantic similarities between different tokens. By fixing the matrix $Z$ to a random configuration, the relative latent geometry of all vocabulary tokens is permanently locked. The only trainable component at the interface is the global transformation $T$, which lacks the capacity to adjust individual token embeddings relative to one another. This severe architectural restriction provides a clear explanation for the massive perplexity degradations observed in Table 1 for all scratch models. Comparing a baseline with fully trainable embeddings to PIT with frozen random embeddings does not constitute a valid or fair evaluation of the tying mechanism.
* Quote: "In scratch-mode, TT and PIT both train stably, with TT remaining lower across most of training in this particular run."
   * Comment: The phrasing "remaining lower across most of training" severely understates the catastrophic impact of the frozen random embeddings. The perplexity gap is not a minor fluctuation, but a massive degradation from 18.3 to 65.0 for the 1.17B parameter model. This massive divergence in performance indicates that the PIT models are fundamentally incapable of learning an effective token space from scratch under these constraints. Framing this outcome as merely "training stably" while ignoring the crippling loss of representational capacity is highly misleading. A method that fundamentally breaks a model's ability to learn word semantics cannot be validated simply because its failure mode is numerically stable.



## Item 3: Tautological evaluation of token-interface consistency

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: I am criticizing the paper for presenting a tautological evaluation of input-side vs. output-side semantic alignment, as it merely measures a mathematical identity enforced by the method's construction. This criticism refers to Section 5.5 (Results On Token-Interface Consistency) and Table 2.
* Evaluation criteria: Conclusions

#### Evidence
* Quote: "For PIT, $B_{in}$ and $B_{out}$ coincide with the shared orthonormal memory $Z$ by construction up to numerical precision."
   * Comment: The evaluation extracts the orthonormal bases $B_{in}$ and $B_{out}$ using polar decompositions of the embedding and unembedding matrices. However, PIT explicitly defines the embedding as $E = Z T^{-1}$ and the unembedding as $W_{out}^T = Z T^T$, where $Z$ is constrained to be orthonormal and $T$ is symmetric positive-definite. Because both $T$ and $T^{-1}$ are symmetric positive-definite, the mathematical polar decomposition of both $E$ and $W_{out}^T$ will invariably yield $Z$ as the unique orthonormal factor. Consequently, the distance metrics computed between $B_{in}$ and $B_{out}$ are merely comparing the identical matrix $Z$ to itself. The $0.0000$ values in Table 2 simply reflect this mathematical identity rather than an empirical finding, rendering the evaluation tautological.
* Quote: "Table 2 reports input-side vs. output-side semantic alignment. PIT reduces all alignment errors to near numerical precision, consistent with the shared-memory construction."
   * Comment: Framing these zero-valued errors as a successful reduction in alignment error misleads the reader into interpreting this as an empirical achievement. Since the method forces $B_{in}$ and $B_{out}$ to be identically $Z$ by algebraic definition, any deviation from zero would strictly indicate a software bug or floating-point inaccuracy. It is logically unsound to evaluate a method's superiority by measuring a constraint that the method explicitly hardcodes. While it is true that this consistency is a feature of the shared-memory construction, it does not provide any empirical evidence that this enforced constraint benefits the model's actual language modeling capabilities. A valid empirical evaluation must assess the downstream effects of this constraint, not redundantly verify that the algebraic equations were implemented correctly.



## Item 4: Misattribution of poor downstream adaptation performance

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: I am criticizing the paper for incorrectly attributing the poor downstream adaptation performance of its scratch-mode models to a lack of degrees of freedom in LoRA, while ignoring that the pretrained base models have drastically worse perplexity. This refers to Section 5.6 (Results on LM Post-Training).
* Evaluation criteria: Conclusions

#### Evidence
* Quote: "In scratch-mode, TT is slightly better across the board in this set of runs. A plausible explanation is that, for these scratch checkpoints, the LoRA adaptation benefits more from the extra degrees of freedom implicit in transpose tying, while PIT’s stricter interface constraint can mildly limit how the update reshapes the token readout."
   * Comment: The performance gap in downstream tasks for scratch models is much more naturally explained by the vast disparity in the quality of the pretrained base models. As shown in Table 1, the scratch-mode PIT Llama-1.17B model achieves a pretraining perplexity of 64.984, compared to the TT baseline's 18.303. A base model with nearly three times the perplexity is fundamentally a much weaker language model with poorly learned representations. Attributing the downstream shortfalls to PIT's stricter interface constraint limiting how LoRA reshapes the token readout completely overlooks this glaring deficiency. It is invalid to draw conclusions about adaptation flexibility when the baseline model is drastically superior to the proposed method's model before any fine-tuning occurs.
* Quote: "Overall, PIT looks most useful as a safety and robustness bias for continued training and lightweight updates on pretrained models, rather than as a universally dominant choice for scratch models."
   * Comment: Characterizing PIT as not being a "universally dominant choice" for scratch models is a profound understatement of the experimental evidence. The empirical results demonstrate that PIT, as implemented with frozen random embeddings, effectively breaks the model's ability to train from scratch. A method that triples the perplexity of a 1.17B parameter language model should be classified as a failure in that specific training regime. By softening the language to suggest it is simply not the dominant choice, the authors obscure the severe negative impact their method has on scratch training. Conclusions regarding the method's utility must transparently acknowledge when the technique is fundamentally incompatible with a given training setup.



## Item 5: Inconsistent reporting of vocabulary size in experimental setup

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: I am criticizing the paper for reporting contradictory values regarding the vocabulary size used in the scratch models, creating ambiguity in the experimental setup. This criticism refers to Appendix A.1 and Table 3.
* Evaluation criteria: Data and methodology

#### Evidence
* Quote: "All models share: (i) the GPT-2 BPE tokenizer with vocabulary size V = 50,257, (ii) tied input/output embeddings (weight tying)..."
   * Comment: Section A.1 explicitly states that all models use a vocabulary size of 50,257, which corresponds to the standard GPT-2 tokenizer. In contrast, the caption for Table 3, which details the specific architectural configurations and parameter scaling for the scratch models, claims a vocabulary size of 32,000. This discrepancy directly affects the reproducibility of the experiments and the accuracy of the reported parameter budgets. For example, the claim that tied embeddings reclaim parameters effectively depends heavily on the exact vocabulary size used in the calculations. This contradiction makes it unclear which tokenizer and vocabulary size were actually employed during the pretraining of the scratch models, undermining the transparency of the methodology.
* Quote: "Table 3. Architectural sweet spots for scratch models, vocabulary size V=32,000, gated GQA with dhead=64, and SwiGLU."
   * Comment: If the scratch models were indeed trained with a vocabulary size of 32,000, this fundamentally breaks the comparability with the teacher-mode models that use the 50,257 vocabulary. Changing the vocabulary size alters the density of the embedding space and the relative difficulty of the language modeling objective. Furthermore, a different vocabulary size implies a different underlying tokenizer, which can significantly skew perplexity measurements across different model families. Without clarifying whether this value is a typographical error or an actual change in the experimental setup, readers cannot confidently assess the validity of the scratch-mode results. Accurate and consistent reporting of such foundational hyperparameters is essential for ensuring that the findings are robust and reproducible.

title: According to Me: Long-Term Personalized Referential Memory QA
review:
## Item 1: Insufficient Test Set Size for ATM-Bench-Hard Claims

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The paper draws major conclusions about the limitations of state-of-the-art models based on their performance on the ATM-Bench-Hard subset, which is statistically too small to provide robust or reliable evaluation metrics.
* Evaluation criteria: Conclusions
* Which component of the paper the criticism refers to: Section 5.2 (Main Findings) and Appendix C.1 (Table 6).

#### Evidence
* Quote: "Notably, on the curated hard set (ATM-Bench-Hard), the current best system falls short of 20% accuracy."
   * Comment: The authors present the poor performance on the ATM-Bench-Hard subset as a cornerstone finding of the paper, using it to demonstrate the limitations of current state-of-the-art systems. By emphasizing this severe accuracy drop, they position this hard set as a critical benchmark for motivating and directing future research in long-term memory QA. However, placing such high emphasis on this specific subset requires the underlying dataset to be large enough to yield statistically significant and reproducible evaluation metrics. Without a sufficiently sized evaluation corpus, the observed performance gap between different models could easily be dominated by random noise or specific idiosyncrasies of a handful of examples. A rigorous benchmark must ensure that its hardest test cases are numerous enough to provide a stable signal for iterative model development.
* Quote: "Table 6. Qtype counts. [...] ATM-Bench-Hard [...] number 6 [...] list_recall 12 [...] open_end 7"
   * Comment: The provided breakdown of question types in Table 6 explicitly reveals that the ATM-Bench-Hard subset consists of exactly 25 questions in total. Reporting percentage-based accuracies on a denominator of 25 is highly problematic, as a single question altering its prediction shifts the system's overall score by a massive 4%. This extremely small sample size makes any comparative claims between models statistically unreliable, as minor variations in reasoning or generation could cause dramatic swings in the leaderboard rankings. Evaluating robust capabilities like multi-evidence aggregation requires a much larger and more diverse set of hard queries to draw meaningful conclusions. Establishing a "challenging" tier for a benchmark with only 25 instances ultimately fails to provide the necessary rigor expected in a new dataset contribution.



## Item 2: Failure to Report the Introduced Recall@kGT Metric

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The methodology explicitly defines a custom retrieval metric to account for varying ground-truth evidence sizes, but this metric is entirely omitted from the experimental results.
* Evaluation criteria: Data and methodology
* Which component of the paper the criticism refers to: Section 3.4 (Evaluation Metrics) and Section 5 (Experiments).

#### Evidence
* Quote: "We report Recall@k, defined as the fraction of ground-truth evidence retrieved among the top-k results, and Recall@kGT, with k set to the number of ground-truth evidence items."
   * Comment: The methodology section clearly introduces Recall@kGT as a designated evaluation metric for assessing the retrieval components of the evaluated memory systems. This metric is particularly appropriate and necessary for this benchmark because queries require varying amounts of evidence, making a static k value less informative than evaluating recall exactly at the ground-truth length. Introducing a custom or specifically parameterized metric creates an expectation that it will be utilized to provide deeper insights into the systems' dynamic retrieval capabilities. Proposing an evaluation criterion but failing to follow through with its application indicates a disconnect between the planned methodology and the executed experiments. This omission weakens the transparency of the evaluation protocol and leaves a gap in the promised analysis.
* Quote: "Table 3. Comparison of memory systems. [...] QS R@10 Joint@10"
   * Comment: Despite the explicit methodological commitment to reporting Recall@kGT, a thorough examination of Table 3, Table 5, and the surrounding text reveals that only R@10 is consistently reported. There is no trace of the Recall@kGT metric anywhere in the experimental results or the supplementary appendix. Given that the ATM-Bench-Hard subset requires an average of 6.3 evidence items, relying solely on a generous top-10 retrieval cutoff (R@10) obscures whether models can precisely isolate the necessary evidence without over-retrieving. By completely omitting a formally defined metric from the final manuscript, the paper fails to deliver a complete and transparent presentation of its data and methodology. Readers are left unable to verify the models' precision and recall characteristics under the stricter ground-truth threshold.



## Item 3: Conflation of Inference Latency and Index Construction Cost

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The paper erroneously categorizes the query-time inference latency of cross-encoder reranking models as an offline indexing cost, demonstrating a fundamental misunderstanding of the retrieval pipeline.
* Evaluation criteria: Clarity and context
* Which component of the paper the criticism refers to: Appendix E.3 (Indexing cost).

#### Evidence
* Quote: "E.3. Indexing cost [...] Index construction time increases substantially with model size: all-MiniLM-L6-v2, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, Qwen3-Embedding-4B, and Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B require approximately 10 seconds, 1 minute, 20 minutes, and 40 minutes, respectively."
   * Comment: In this section, the authors accurately describe the time required to process the memory corpus and build an offline retrieval index using various embedding models. Index construction is fundamentally a pre-computation step where all documents in the corpus are mapped to a vector space before any user queries are processed. Tracking this offline computational overhead is a standard and useful practice for comparing the scalability of different dense retriever architectures. By explicitly framing this as "Indexing cost" and "Index construction time", the authors set a clear context regarding the offline computational burden of their memory pipeline. This correctly reflects the standard terminology used in information retrieval literature for the initial document ingestion phase.
* Quote: "Reranking adds further overhead, with the 0.6B and 4B rerankers taking approximately 10 minutes and 50 minutes, respectively."
   * Comment: The authors mistakenly categorize the time consumed by the cross-encoder reranking models as an addition to the offline index construction overhead. Cross-encoder rerankers operate entirely at inference time by jointly scoring a specific user query against a small set of retrieved candidate documents. Because they strictly require the query text to function, they cannot be used to pre-compute an offline index over the standalone document corpus. The reported 10 to 50 minutes actually represent the cumulative query inference latency across the entire evaluation dataset, not the time taken to build a searchable index. Conflating online inference latency with offline indexing cost demonstrates a significant misunderstanding of the retrieval pipeline and compromises the clarity and accuracy of the methodology reporting.



## Item 4: Unsubstantiated Claims Regarding Memory Representations

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The authors attribute the performance gap between Schema-Guided Memory (SGM) and Descriptive Memory (DM) solely to data formatting, ignoring that SGM's rigid schema acts as a stronger prompt that extracts fundamentally richer factual content.
* Evaluation criteria: Conclusions
* Which component of the paper the criticism refers to: Section 4.2 (Memory Ingestion) and Section 5.2 (Main Findings).

#### Evidence
* Quote: "Notably, SGM and DM encompass the same information and differ only in how this information is formatted."
   * Comment: The authors assert that the performance differences between Schema-Guided Memory (SGM) and Descriptive Memory (DM) stem purely from the structural formatting of identical underlying data. This claim implies a strictly controlled experimental setup where the informational content is held perfectly constant while only the presentation layout is varied. Drawing conclusions about the efficacy of structured versus unstructured memory fundamentally relies on this strict assumption of informational equivalence. If one format inadvertently contains richer or more precise details than the other, any observed downstream performance gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the structural format alone. Therefore, the validity of this comparative analysis hinges entirely on whether both representations genuinely encapsulate the exact same facts extracted from the raw memory corpus.
* Quote: "SGM represents each memory item as a set of text-based key-value fields defined under a fixed schema S. [...] S includes fields such as time, location, entities, OCR, and tags."
   * Comment: The definition of SGM contradicts the premise of informational equivalence because it enforces a rigid schema that actively prompts the ingesting Vision-Language Model to extract highly specific metadata. Asking a VLM to explicitly populate fields for "OCR" text and "entities" serves as a powerful and targeted information extraction directive. In contrast, a generic prompt asking for a "natural-language description" (DM) is far more likely to yield a high-level summary that glosses over granular background text or minor objects. Consequently, SGM likely outperforms DM because its structured prompt elicits a much more comprehensive factual extraction from the raw data, rather than just organizing identical facts more efficiently. By ignoring this critical disparity in extraction completeness, the authors draw an invalid and confounded conclusion about the inherent superiority of the key-value formatting itself.



## Item 5: Contradictory Reporting of Benchmark Corpus Size

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The paper presents inconsistent counts regarding the total size of its primary dataset, with summary tables claiming a substantially larger corpus than the detailed statistical breakdowns support.
* Evaluation criteria: Data and methodology
* Which component of the paper the criticism refers to: Section 3.2 (Table 1) and Section 3.3 (Table 2).

#### Evidence
* Quote: "Table 1. Comparison of ATM-Bench with other memory and long-context QA benchmarks. [...] ATM-Bench [...] #Mem 12k"
   * Comment: Table 1 serves as the primary comparative overview of the proposed ATM-Bench against existing datasets in the literature, establishing its relative scale and complexity. In this highly visible summary, the authors explicitly claim that the benchmark contains 12,000 memory items under the #Mem column. Providing precise and consistent dataset statistics is a fundamental requirement for a benchmark paper, as it allows researchers to understand the exact scope of the evaluation corpus. The figure of 12k is presented as a definitive metric of the benchmark's size and is used to position the dataset as a substantial contribution to the field. Readers rely on these high-level summary tables to quickly grasp the scale of the data before diving into the detailed methodology and experimental setup.
* Quote: "Table 2. Corpus statistics. [...] Email 6,741 [...] Image 3,759 [...] Video 533"
   * Comment: The detailed breakdown of the corpus provided in Table 2 directly contradicts the overarching claim made in Table 1 regarding the total size of the dataset. When summing the exact counts of emails, images, and videos explicitly listed here, the total number of memory items comes out to precisely 11,033. A discrepancy of nearly a thousand items between the detailed breakdown and the summary table cannot be dismissed as standard rounding, as 11,033 would conventionally round to 11k rather than 12k. This inconsistency in reporting the fundamental size of the primary dataset introduces unnecessary confusion and casts doubt on the rigorousness of the data management. A benchmark paper must ensure complete alignment between its summary claims and its detailed statistical breakdowns to maintain methodological transparency and accuracy.

title: FlattenGPT: Depth Compression for Transformer with Layer Flattening
review:
## Item 1: Dimensional mismatch in the MLP pruning algorithm

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The mathematical and algorithmic formulation of the MLP channel pruning operation contains impossible dimension mismatches that prevent the method from functioning as described.
* Evaluation criteria: Data and methodology, Validity.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "$\hat{W}_D = W_D + S_k \Delta \hat{W}_D$"
   * Comment: This equation formulates the down-projection matrix of the pruned MLP block by adding the original matrix $W_D$ to a compensation term. In the flattened MLP block, the original $W_D$ possesses dimensions of $2d_{int} \times d$, where $d_{int}$ is the intermediate width of a single block. The term $S_k \Delta \hat{W}_D$ projects the $k \times d$ compensation matrix back into the $2d_{int}$ space, meaning the resulting $\hat{W}_D$ also retains a size of $2d_{int} \times d$. By keeping this dimension unchanged, the algorithm fails to achieve its primary objective of compressing the parameter count of the down-projection layer. Furthermore, since the corresponding up-projection layers are successfully pruned to output $k$ channels, attempting to multiply this $T \times k$ intermediate activation by a $2d_{int} \times d$ down-projection matrix creates a fatal dimension mismatch that fundamentally breaks the forward pass.
* Quote: "return $(W_u, W_g, W_D) \leftarrow \left(W_u S_k, W_g S_k, W_D + \left(S_k^\top C_\psi S_k + \lambda I\right)^{-1} S_k^\top C_\psi \left(I - S_k S_k^\top\right) W_D\right)$"
   * Comment: The pseudo-code attempts to circumvent the issue in Equation 13 by directly adding the compensation term to $W_D$, but this introduces an even more severe mathematical error. The compensation term $\left(S_k^\top C_\psi S_k + \lambda I\right)^{-1} S_k^\top C_\psi \left(I - S_k S_k^\top\right) W_D$ correctly resolves to a matrix of shape $k \times d$, matching the compressed inner dimension of the pruned layer. However, the original $W_D$ matrix remains at its full flattened size of $2d_{int} \times d$. Adding a $2d_{int} \times d$ matrix directly to a $k \times d$ matrix is an undefined mathematical operation, rendering the algorithm impossible to implement as described. To yield a mathematically sound and properly compressed layer, the formula should map the retained weights directly to the compressed space by replacing $W_D$ with $S_k^\top W_D$ prior to the addition.



## Item 2: Invalid attention head importance metric yields a matrix

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The proposed MHA pruning importance metric mathematically yields a sequence-dependent matrix rather than the scalar score required by the pruning algorithm, making it unusable.
* Evaluation criteria: Validity, Appropriate use of statistics and treatment of uncertainties.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "$f_i =\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}} \left[ \text{Softmax} \left( \psi_r \left(X W_{Q,i}\right) \psi_r^\top \left(X W_{K,i}\right) \right) X W_{V,i} \text{diag} \left( W_{O,i} W_{O,i}^\top \right)^{1/2} \right]$"
   * Comment: The proposed importance metric $f_i$ intends to quantify the impact of each attention head on the network's output to guide the pruning process. However, the expression inside the expectation mathematically evaluates to a two-dimensional matrix of shape $T \times d_h$, where $T$ is the sequence length and $d_h$ is the head dimension. This occurs because the $T \times T$ attention probabilities are multiplied by the $T \times d_h$ value matrix, and then scaled by a $d_h$-dimensional diagonal vector. Without a subsequent reduction operation, such as an L2 norm or a sum across the sequence and feature dimensions, the metric fails to produce a single aggregated value. Consequently, the equation outputs a sequence-dependent matrix rather than a standalone numerical score, which completely invalidates its intended utility for directly comparing different heads.
* Quote: "Let $S_k \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$ be the matrix that selects the top $k$ heads based on $\{f_i\}$ scores"
   * Comment: This step of the algorithm relies on sorting the $\{f_i\}$ scores to select the most critical attention heads for preservation. Because Equation 12 yields a matrix rather than a scalar for each head, it is mathematically impossible to rank them in a one-dimensional order without introducing an arbitrary aggregation scheme not defined in the text. Furthermore, the notation $S_k \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$ is highly irregular and confusing for a matrix intended to simply select $k$ heads out of a total of $H$ available heads. In typical pruning literature, identifying the top components requires a robust scalar proxy for importance, meaning the implementation of this algorithm would require substantial deviations from the presented equations. These combined issues indicate a significant breakdown in the formalization and reproducibility of the MHA channel pruning methodology.



## Item 3: Dimensionally invalid matrix operations in the flattened MLP formulation

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The mathematical definition of the flattened MLP block omits a mandatory element-wise multiplication operator, leading to a dimensionally impossible equation.
* Evaluation criteria: Clarity and context, Validity.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "$\text{MLP}^{\ell-1,\ell} (X) =X\tilde{W}_u^{\ell-1} \psi_g \left(X\tilde{W}_g^{\ell-1}\right) W_D^{\ell-1} +X\tilde{W}_u^\ell \psi_g \left(X\tilde{W}_g^\ell\right) W_D^\ell$"
   * Comment: This equation attempts to formally define the output of the newly flattened, double-width gated MLP block by summing the parallel contributions of the constituent layers. In the expression, both the up-projection mapping $X\tilde{W}_u$ and the gated activation $\psi_g \left(X\tilde{W}_g\right)$ naturally produce matrices of size $T \times d_{int}$. By writing these two terms adjacently without specifying an element-wise multiplication operator, the notation dictates a standard matrix multiplication. A standard matrix multiplication between two $T \times d_{int}$ matrices is dimensionally impossible, breaking the core mathematical definition of the module. This error severely undermines the clarity and precision of the methodology, potentially confusing readers attempting to faithfully implement or build upon the flattened architecture.
* Quote: "$\psi_s \left(XW_U^\ell\right) = XW_u^\ell \odot \psi_g \left(XW_g^\ell\right)$ where $\psi_g$ is the gate activation."
   * Comment: Earlier in the preliminary section, the authors correctly utilize the Hadamard product ($\odot$) to combine the up-projection and the gated activation for a standard gated MLP layer. The conspicuous absence of this operator in Equation 11 reveals a severe inconsistency in the manuscript's mathematical notation. While it is conceptually obvious that the authors intended for the flattened layer to follow the same element-wise gating mechanism as the original blocks, the formal equations do not reflect this reality. Such notational sloppiness in the definition of the paper's primary architectural contribution is unacceptable, as a strict interpretation of the text yields a non-functional network. Ensuring that foundational mathematical formulas are both internally consistent and physically possible is a baseline requirement for a reproducible methodology.



## Item 4: Contradiction in Layer Selection Metric

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The layer selection algorithm employs a similarity metric that contradicts its stated theoretical justification, evaluating entire blocks instead of adjacent inputs.
* Evaluation criteria: Validity, Clarity and context.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "...where $S_{i,j}$ denote the cosine similarity between the input feature of layer $i$ and the output feature of layer $j$."
   * Comment: The paper relies on the similarity matrix $S_{i,j}$ to identify adjacent blocks that are suitable candidates for layer flattening.
